title: Kashmir Shaivism opening (the Shiva Sutras)
hook: a teacher dreams of words cut into a rock, and the first of them says consciousness is the self

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the Shiva Sahasranama with Mahadeva, and the boy who wanted milk. Which name did you keep, and when did it come back to you? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-nine.
screen: `MAHADEVA GATHERS THE NAMES.` · `A NEW BOOK OPENS.`

segments.voice: A rock on a mountainside in Kashmir. That's where this story says a teaching was waiting. Tradition remembers a teacher named Vasugupta, a devotee of Shiva, who had a dream. In it, Shiva told him that on a certain mountain there was a great stone, and on the stone, words were cut: short lines of teaching that had been forgotten. Vasugupta woke up. And now he has to decide what a dream is worth. Today we start a new book, the Shiva Sutras, and with it the opening of Kashmir Shaivism.
screen: `A ROCK IN KASHMIR.` → `VASUGUPTA'S DREAM.` → `THE SHIVA SUTRAS.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Vasugupta went. He climbed to the place from the dream, found the stone, and touched it, and it turned over, showing the lines carved underneath. Some commentators tell it differently, saying Shiva taught him in the dream itself. Either way, the tradition treats the Shiva Sutras as given, not invented. A sutra is a thread, a line so short it has to be unpacked by a teacher. And the very first thread of this book is two words: chaitanyam atma. Consciousness is the self. Sit with how strange and how simple that is. It doesn't say you have consciousness, the way you have a phone or a cold. It says you are it. Not the body, not the name, not the job title, not the mood you woke up in. Those come and go. The awareness that notices them coming and going: that's the self. And Kashmir Shaivism takes one more step. That consciousness isn't a small private light in each head. It's Shiva's own, one consciousness, appearing as everything and everyone. So the first line of the book is also a line about God. Commentators in this tradition, like Kshemaraja, linger over these two words, and read the rest of the book as unfolding from them. Over the last several days, the sahasranama gave Shiva a long string of names, each one a door. Here the tradition goes the other way: no long list, just one thread, pointing not out at Shiva but in, at whoever is listening.
screen: `THE STONE TURNS OVER.` · `SUTRA: A THREAD TO UNPACK.` · `CHAITANYAM ATMA.` · `ONE CONSCIOUSNESS, SHIVA'S OWN.` · then, large: `CONSCIOUSNESS IS THE SELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice the noticing. Sit, and let the breath settle. Let sounds come in: a car, a fan, your own breathing. Let thoughts come in too. Each time something appears, say to yourself, softly, noticed. Then, every so often, turn around and ask: what is doing the noticing? Don't answer with a word. Just rest in whatever is aware, for a breath or two. If you pray, you can hold the first sutra, consciousness is the self, as your line. The bell holds the time.
Kashmir Shaivism opening. A new book, the Shiva Sutras, said to be found on a rock, and its first thread: chaitanyam atma, consciousness is the self.
Your line: Kashmir Shaivism opening, the Shiva Sutras. Today, when a mood takes over, notice the one who notices the mood. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: In the Kashmir Shaiva tradition the Shiva Sutras are studied with a teacher and a commentary, such as Kshemaraja's, one short line at a time.

trapdoor: what you thought: Kashmir Shaivism is Shiva worship that happens in Kashmir.
what it means: a teaching that opens with one line: consciousness is the self, and that consciousness is Shiva's own.
what a scholar hears: Shiva Sutra 1.1, chaitanyam atma, revealed to Vasugupta by tradition, and unpacked by commentators such as Kshemaraja.

notes: First of this writer's three Kashmir Shaivism days (1139–1141); day 1142, already written, teaches sutras 3.9–3.11 (the dancer, the stage, the spectators), so these days stay with the opening sutras.

Vasugupta's dream and the stone that turned over (the Shankaropala) are told in Kshemaraja's Vimarshini; the 'some commentators' line refers to the version in which Shiva teaches the sutras in the dream (associated with Bhaskara's tradition). Confirm both attributions.
Sanskrit for 1.1 given as चैतन्यमात्मा (caitanyam ātmā). Confirm the sandhi and transliteration.
'Kshemaraja spends pages on these two words' is a general description; confirm or soften.
No dates are given for Vasugupta or Kshemaraja on purpose.
